messages.subject: Transformation bias using log-link?
parts:
Hi all,

I've been running a bunch of hierarchical spatio-temporal models on heavily over-disperse data using a negative Binomial distribution. The fitted values of the model are always systematically over predicting by an exponent of roughly 1.5.

If I transform the fitted values to the power of 0.65 everything looks perfect, the residuals are homogeneous, and the forecasting power is more accurate. However I do not know how I can justify this transformation in my research.

I have read a few papers about transformation bias when using log links, but it seems like this should not be an issue with this Bayesian approach?

Is there any way I can adjust my model to correct or account for this bias during the fitting process? Or is it acceptable to manually correct the bias afterwards? Note that this bias occurs on both training data and out of sample testing data.

Any help or advice would be greatly appreciated - R-INLA is amazing and I look forward to promoting it through this research.

Thanks in advance,

Hayden

parts:
On 27 Feb 2017, at 20:05, Hayden Rabel <hayden...@gmail.com> wrote:
Should E(exp(summary.linear.predictor)) be equivalent to summary.fitted.values in this case? I am finding slight discrepancies between these two vectors.

Hi,
 adding a few comments to what Håvard mentioned:
Yes, in theory the expectation (mean) in summary.fitted.values should be the same as E(exp(linearpredictor)), since they are calculated in different ways, there will always be numerical discrepancies. When you say "slight", precisely what do you mean? Anything that's much smaller than the width of the quantile based prediction interval is ignorable. If the difference is a noticeable fraction of that, then there might be cause for concern.

Precisely how are you assessing the posteriors? What kind of residuals? Because expectations and link functions are not commutative, E(g(x)) is not g(E(x)), one always needs to be extremely careful in comparing like-for-like.  If you only use the quantiles of the inla output, and no expectations and variances, and evaluate only such prediction intervals, do you still see what you called overprediction?  There might still be issues with highly dispersed distributions, but quantiles are at least much more stable, in theory, than expectations and variances.

If your need to assess point estimates, perhaps the posterior medians are more useful that the posterior means?  Those should be assessed using e.g. mean absolute deviation of the residuals.

Finn L

When using exp(E(summary.linear.predictor)) the over-prediction mentioned previously is inflated even further?

Could this have something to do with the way I have include the effort term in my model?

I use offset(E = log(E)) and the default parameterisation of the negative Binomial likelihood (variant = 0). Should I be enforcing control.family = list(variant = 1) instead?

Thanks again,

Hayden

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Transformation bias using log-link?

On Tue, 2017-02-28 at 17:42 +1300, Hayden Rabel wrote:
> Hi Håvard,
>
> That may be the problem, I am using the stable version of INLA
> currently. I will upgrade to testing first thing in the morning.
>
> Do you have documentation I can read about the parameters for the
> pc.mgamma distribution?

good point...

here is how to do this.

Poisson(exp(eta) * s)

where s ~ Gamma(1/delta,1/delta)

is neg binom, with size = 1/delta (see R doc for nbinom).

then we construct the PC-prior for delta; see the upcoming discussion
paper in StatSci. (which you have to read to understand the pc prior)

this is the way to simulate 's' for a given value of lambda, which
controls how close s is to 1, ie the simpler Poisson model. the default
choice is lambda=7. the initial value is just the starting value.

lambda = 7
n = 10^6
delta = inla.pc.rgamma(n, lambda = lambda)
s = rgamma(n, shape = 1/delta, rate = 1/delta)
hist(s, n = 100)

hope this helps!
H


--
Håvard Rue
he...@r-inla.org

Should E(exp(summary.linear.predictor)) be equivalent to summary.fitted.values in this case? I am finding slight discrepancies between these two vectors.

Hi,
 adding a few comments to what Håvard mentioned:
Yes, in theory the expectation (mean) in summary.fitted.values should be the same as E(exp(linearpredictor)), since they are calculated in different ways, there will always be numerical discrepancies. When you say "slight", precisely what do you mean? Anything that's much smaller than the width of the quantile based prediction interval is ignorable. If the difference is a noticeable fraction of that, then there might be cause for concern.

Precisely how are you assessing the posteriors? What kind of residuals? Because expectations and link functions are not commutative, E(g(x)) is not g(E(x)), one always needs to be extremely careful in comparing like-for-like.  If you only use the quantiles of the inla output, and no expectations and variances, and evaluate only such prediction intervals, do you still see what you called overprediction?  There might still be issues with highly dispersed distributions, but quantiles are at least much more stable, in theory, than expectations and variances.

If your need to assess point estimates, perhaps the posterior medians are more useful that the posterior means?  Those should be assessed using e.g. mean absolute deviation of the residuals.

Finn L
